newsitem.title: USA: Brown Bros starts inflation index-linked bond fund.
newsitem.headline: Brown Bros starts inflation index-linked bond fund.

text.p: Brown Brothers Harriman & Co on Monday introduced a fund to be comprised primarily of inflation indexed U.S. Treasuries as well as inflation-indexed bonds from other countries and corporations.
The firm said its conventional bond fund, 59 Wall Street Short/Intermediate Fixed Income Fund, will be converted this week to the 59 Wall Street Inflation-Indexed Securities Fund.

The fund currently has $16 million in assets. Brown Brothers partner Jeffrey Schoenfeld said he hoped the no-load fund's assets would grow to $100 million or more by year-end, as investors embrace inflation indexed securities.
"To the extent the equity market declines, people will look to conventional bond funds, index linked bond funds and cash," Schoenfeld said a press luncheon.
The fund, named after Brown Brothers' long-time address, will be distributed through Charles Schwab's One Source Mutual Funds Program, the Fidelity Fundsnetwork and the Jack White No Fee Network.

Schoenfeld noted the fund's portfolio will include at least 65 percent of U.S. Treasury index-linked securities, as well as similar bonds from other countries and corporations and asset-backed and mortgage-backed securities.

Brown Brothers did not participate in the Treasury's auction of 10-year index linked 10-year notes in late January, but has been active in the secondary market, and the firm plans to bid on securities at future auctions, Schoenfeld said.
The Treasury will sell inflation indexed bonds in mid April, when it plans to reopen the January 2007 10-year note.

Christopher Kinney, a manager in Brown Brothers' fixed income group, described the Treasury's inaugural indexed linked note sale January 29 as a "stupendous success" that was five times oversubcribed and awarded at a rate five basis points -- 3.449 percent -- lower than where it had traded at the 1300 EST bidding deadline.

The current 10-year issue is only $7 billion, and will be twice that when the Treasury reopens the January 2007 issue next month. Kinney expects liquidity in the indexed-linked securities market to swell to a robust $200 billion to $300 billion in a few years.

"It's so brand new, it will alter the financial landscape," he said. "There are uncertainties that remain, but this should be a good time to buy if you think inflation risks are tilted to the upside."

Kinney said his study found inflation indexed securities outperform their conventional securities counterpart in times of rising inflation, although, he added, the opposite is true in times of declining inflation.
"The Treasury should have issued these 20 years ago when inflation was high," he said. "It would have saved the government a lot of money."

Schoenfeld said he expects inflation to remain historically low, running at 3.0 percent to 3.5 percent in 1997, edging up to 3.5 percent to 4.0 percent in 1998. He cited technology advances improving productivity and governments around the world working to lower budget deficits -- which coincides with lower inflation -- as reasons prices should stay tame.
Brown Brothers is among a handful of firms offering funds with index-linked securities. Pacific Investement Managing Co launched one in late January. Dreyfuss and 21st Century also offer them.
